label: prop:Buv
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{prop:Buv}
Let $X$ be a connected graph on $n$ vertices. If (i) $M=A$ and $X$ is regular, or (ii) $M=L$, then $B(X)_{u,v}\geq \frac{2}{n}$ for all $u,v\in V(X)$. Moreover, if $u\neq v$, then equality is attained in complete graphs.

title: Proof
body_md:
Suppose that (i) or (ii) holds. So, $E_k= rac{1}{n}\mathbf{J}$ when $M=A$ and $X$ is $k$-regular, and $E_0= rac{1}{n}\mathbf{J}$ when $M=L$. Since $B(X)_{u,u}=1$ for all $u\in V(X)$, it suffices to prove the statement when $u
eq v$. Since $X$ is connected, $M$ has at least two distinct eigenvalues. Set $	heta=k$ when $M=A$ and $X$ is $k$-regular, and $	heta=0$ otherwise so that $(E_	heta)_{u,u}= rac{1}{n}$. Because $E_\lambda$'s sum to $I$ and $u
eq v$, we have $\sum_{\lambda\in{\mathrm{spec}}(M) ackslash\{	heta\}}(E_\lambda)_{u,v}=- rac{1}{n}.$
Thus, there exists $\varnothing
eq S\subseteq {\mathrm{spec}}(M) ackslash\{	heta\}$ such that $(E_\lambda)_{u,v}<0$ for all $\lambda\in S$ and $\sum_{\lambda\in S}(E_\lambda)_{u,v}\leq - rac{1}{n}$. So $ ig|\sum_{\lambda\in S}(E_\lambda)_{u,v}
 ig|\geq rac{1}{n}$. Thus, $B(X)_{u,v}\geq (E_	heta)_{u,u}+ ig| \sum_{\lambda\in S}(E_\lambda)_{u,v} ig|=  rac{2}{n}$, with equality when $X=K_n$.

title: Remark
body_md: It is known that PST is a monogamous relation, i.e., if PST occurs between $u$ and $v$, and also between $u$ and $w$, then $v=w$ \cite{Kay2011}. However, peak state transfer is not monogamous in general. For example, complete graphs admit peak state transfer between any pair of vertices (see Example~\ref{ex:knnn}).

label: ex:path1
title: Example
body_md:
\label{ex:path1}
Let $M=A$. From \cite{Godsil2012}, $P_n$ has PGST between end vertices if and only if the set ${\mathrm{spec}}(A)\cap\mathbb{R}^+$ is linearly independent over $\mathbb{Q}$. Equivalently, $n+1\in\{2^t,p,2p\}$ where $t\geq 1$ is an integer and $p\geq 1$ is a prime, in which case PGST in $P_n$ occurs between $j$ and $n+1-j$ for all $j\in V(P_n)$. In particular, if $n+1\in\{2^t,2p\}$, then $j$ and $n+1-j$ belong to the same parts in $P_n$, and so PGST occurs between them relative to $\{\tau_m\}\subseteq 2\pi\mathbb{Z}$ by Theorem~\ref{thm:pgst}.

title: Remark
body_md: Sedentariness and PGST are known to be mutually exclusive \cite{Monterde2023}. That is, if PGST occurs between $u$ and $v$, then none of them are sedentary, and if $u$ is sedentary, then it cannot be involved in PGST. However, vertex sedentariness and peak state transfer are not necessarily mutually exclusive, i.e., it is possible for a vertex to be sedentary and also be involved in peak state transfer.

label: prop:sedpeak
title: Proposition
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md: By the unitarity of $U_X(t)$, we get $|U_X(t)_{u,u}|^2+|U_X(t)_{u,v}|^2\leq 1$ for all $t\in\mathbb{R}$. Since $u$ is $C$-sedentary, we have $|U_X(t)_{u,u}|\geq C$ for all $t\in\mathbb{R}$. So, $|U_X(t)_{u,v}|^2\leq 1-|U_X(t)_{u,u}|^2\leq 1-C^2$ for all $t\in\mathbb{R}$. Thus, $|U_X(t)_{u,v}|\leq \sqrt{1-C^2}$ for all $t\in\mathbb{R}$. As peak state transfer also occurs between $u$ and $v$ at time $\tau$, $B(X)_{u,v}$ is attained by $|U_X(t)_{u,v}|$ at time $\tau$. Combining these observations yields the result.

label: lem:joinbound
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:joinbound}
Let $M\in\{A,L\}$ and consider  $X\vee Y$, where we assume that $X,Y$ are $k$- and $\ell$-regular graphs, respectively, whenever $M=A$. If $u,v\in V(X)$, then $B(X\vee Y)_{u,v}=B(X)_{u,v}$. Otherwise, $B(X\vee Y)_{u,v}=\frac{2}{n}$ if $M=L$ and $B(X\vee Y)_{u,v}=\frac{2}{\sqrt{\Delta}}$ otherwise.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Let $u,v\in V(X)$. If $M=L$, then (\ref{eq:joinL}) yields
$B(X\vee Y)_{u,v}=\frac{1}{n}+\frac{n_2}{n_1n}+B(X)_{u,v}-\frac{1}{n_1}=B(X)_{u,v}$. If $M=A$, then (\ref{eq:joinA}) yields $B(X\vee Y)_{u,v}=\frac{k-\lambda^-}{n_1\sqrt{\Delta}}-\frac{k-\lambda^+}{n_1\sqrt{\Delta}}+B(X)_{u,v}-\frac{1}{n_1}=B(X)_{u,v}$. Combining these two cases proves the case $u,v\in V(X)$, while the other case is immediate from (\ref{eq:joinL}) and (\ref{eq:joinA}).

label: ex:knnn
title: Example
body_md:
\label{ex:knnn}
Let $m\geq 2$ and $X$ be the balanced complete multipartite graph $K_{m,\ldots,m}$ with $k\geq 2$ parts. We may write $X=\bigvee_k O_m=O_m\vee \big(\bigvee_{k-1} O_m\big)$,
where $O_m$ is the empty graph on $m$ vertices and $\bigvee_{k-1} O_m$ is $m(k-2)$-regular with $m(k-1)$ vertices. Note that 
$\Delta=(0-(m(k-2))^2)+4m(m(k-1))=m^2k^2$. We apply Theorem~\ref{thm:peakstjoin1} with $M=A$ (this also holds for $M=L$ since $X$ is regular). If $u$ and $v$ are adjacent in $X$, 
then peak state transfer occurs between them at time $\tau=\frac{\pi}{mk}$ and $|U(\tau)_{u,v}|=\frac{2}{mk}$. In particular, if $m=2$ (resp., $m=1$), then $X$ is the cocktail party graph on $2k$ vertices (resp., $X=K_k$).

label: ex:pgst1
title: Example
body_md:
\label{ex:pgst1}
Let $X$ be graph on $n_1$ vertices, where we assume that $X$ is $k$-regular when $M=A$. Suppose $X$ has PGST between $u$ and $v$ relative to $\{\tau_m\}\subseteq 2\pi\mathbb{Z}$ (see Theorem~\ref{thm:pgst} for sufficient conditions for this to occur). Since $\lim_{m\rightarrow\infty}e^{i\tau_m p}=1$ for any integer $p$, PGST occurs between $u$ and $v$ in $X\vee Y$ relative to $\{\tau_m\}$ for any graph $Y$ when $M=L$. Meanwhile, when $M=A$, if $\lambda^+,\lambda^-$ are integers, then PGST occurs between $u$ and $v$ in $X\vee Y$ relative to $\{\tau_m\}$. For example, if $X=\operatorname{Cay}(\mathbb{Z}_{2^r},S)$ in Example~\ref{ex:Cn}, then PGST occurs between $u$ and $v=u+2^{r-1}$ in $X$ relative to $\{\tau_m\}\subseteq 2\pi\mathbb{Z}$. So if $Y$ is $\ell$-regular with $n_2$ vertices and $(\ell-|S|)^2+2^{r+2}n_2$ is a perfect square, then $X\vee Y$ has PGST between $u$ and $v$ relative to $\{\tau_m\}$.
head: environment

title: Example
body_md: Suppose the same hypothesis in Example~\ref{ex:pgst1} hold, except we assume  $\{\tau_m\}\subseteq (2\mathbb{Z}+1)\frac{\pi}{2}$. If $n,n_2\equiv d\pmod{4}$ where $d\in\{0,2\}$, then $\lim_{m\rightarrow\infty}e^{i\tau_mn}=\lim_{m\rightarrow\infty}e^{i\tau_mn_2}=\pm 1$, and so PGST occurs between $u$ and $v$ in $X\vee Y$ relative to $\{\tau_m\}$ when $M=L$. For the case $M=A$, if $\lambda^+,\lambda^-$ are integers and $k,\lambda^+,\lambda^-\equiv d\pmod{4}$, where $d\in\{0,2\}$, then $\lim_{m\rightarrow\infty}e^{i\tau_m\lambda^+}=\lim_{m\rightarrow\infty}e^{i\tau_m\lambda^-}=\lim_{m\rightarrow\infty}e^{i\tau_mk}=\pm 1$, and so PGST occurs between $u$ and $v$ in $X\vee Y$ relative to $\{\tau_m\}$. Note that $n_2$ and $\ell$ may be chosen appropriately to obtain $k,\lambda^+,\lambda^-\equiv d\pmod{4}$ (for instance, $n_2$ and $\ell$ may be chosen such that $k=\ell\equiv d\pmod{4}$ and $\sqrt{n_1n_2}\equiv 0\pmod{4}$). By way of example, we may take $X=\operatorname{Cay}(\mathbb{Z}_{n_1},S\cup\{\frac{n_1}{4},\frac{3n_1}{4}\})$ in Example~\ref{ex:Cn1}, where $n_1=2^r$ and $|S\cap S_{n_1}(d)|\equiv 0\pmod{4}$ (this happens if $S$ has four elements from each of $S_{n_1}(d)$ for all $1\leq d<\frac{n_1}{4}$). As $|S|\equiv 0\pmod{4}$, we get $k=|S\cup\{\frac{n_1}{4},\frac{3n_1}{4}\}|\equiv 2\pmod 4$. So, if $\lambda^+,\lambda^-\equiv 2\pmod{4}$, then PGST occurs between $u$ and $v=u+\frac{n}{2}$ in $X\vee Y$ relative to $\{\tau_m\}$.

label: thm:pgstpal
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{thm:pgstpal}
Suppose that PST occurs between $u$ and $v$ in $X$ at time $\tau$ and between $x$ and $y$ in $Y$ at time $\tau'$ such that $\{1,\frac{\tau'}{\tau}\}$ is a linearly independent set over $\mathbb{Q}$. Then there exists a sequence $\{m_r\}$ of odd integers such that $\lim_{r\rightarrow\infty}|U_Y(m_r\tau)_{x,y}|=1$. Consequently, PGST occurs between $(u,x)$ and $(v,y)$ in $X\square Y$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Let $\{1,\frac{\tau'}{\tau}\}$ be a linearly independent set over $\mathbb{Q}$. By Theorem~\ref{thm:kron}, for each $\epsilon>0$, there are integers $q,p$ such that $|q(\frac{\tau'}{\tau})-p-\frac{1}{2}(1-\frac{\tau'}{\tau})|<\frac{\epsilon}{2\tau}\pmod{2\pi}$. Equivalently, $|(2q+1) \tau'-(2p+1)\tau|<\epsilon \pmod{2\pi}$.
Thus, for each $\epsilon>0$, there exist sequences of odd integers $\{2q_r+1\}$ and $\{2p_r+1\}$ satisfying the property $\lim_{r\rightarrow\infty}|(2q_r+1) \tau'-(2p_r+1)\tau|=0$. Now, since PST occurs between $x$ and $y$ in $Y$ at every odd multiple of $\tau'$, we get
$|U_Y((2q_r+1)\tau')_{x,y}|=1$ for each $r$, and because $|U_Y(t)_{x,y}|$ is continuous, we get $\lim_{r\rightarrow\infty}|U_Y((2p_r+1)\tau)_{x,y}|=1$. Combining this with (\ref{eq:cartprod}) yields the desired conclusion.
head: environment

title: Example
body_md:
For all integers $m\geq 1$, $P_3^{\square m}$ admits PST at time $\frac{\pi}{\sqrt{2}}$. If $X$ is a regular graph admitting PST at time $\tau'$, then $\tau'=\frac{\pi}{g}$ for some integer $g\geq 1$. Applying Theorem~\ref{thm:pgstpal}, we obtain PGST in 
$(P_3^{\square m})\square X$. In particular, if $X=H(d,2)$, then $\tau'=\frac{\pi}{2}$, and so
$(P_3^{\square m})\square H(d,2)$ has PGST for all integers $m,d\geq 1$.

title: Proof
body_md: If $|U_{X^c}(t)_{u,v}|\geq |U_X(t)_{u,v}|$, then $g_{u,v}(t)=|U_{X^c}(t)_{u,v}|-|U_X(t)_{u,v}|\leq B(X^c)_{u,v}-|U_X(t)_{u,v}|\leq B(X^c)_{u,v}$. Otherwise, $g_{u,v}(t)\leq B(X)_{u,v}$. Thus, $g_{u,v}(t)\leq b$ for all $t\in\mathbb{R}$. The bounds for $f_{u,v}(t)$ follow from (\ref{eq:bounding}) and the triangle inequality.

label: prop:regupperbound1

title: Proof
body_md: Since $U_X(-t)=\overline{U_X(t)}$, we get $U_X(-t)_{u,v}=\overline{U_X(t)_{u,v}}$, and so $|U_X(-t)_{u,v}|=|U_X(t)_{u,v}|$. By the triangle inequality, $g_{u,v}(t)=||U_{X^c}(t)_{u,v}|-|U_X(-t)_{u,v}||\leq |U_{X^c}(t)_{u,v}-e^{it\delta}U_X(-t)_{u,v}|=f_{u,v}(t).$

label: ex:k2n
title: Example
body_md:
\label{ex:k2n}
Let $M=A$. The following hold.
\begin{enumerate}
\item Let $n$ be an even perfect square and $u$ be the central vertex of $X=K_{1,r}$. Then $u$ is isolated in $X^c$, and so $U_{X^c}(t)_{u,u}=1$ for all $t$. Since $U_{X}(t)_{u,u}=\cos(\sqrt{r}t)$, $f_{u,u}\big(\pi\big)=
\big|1-e^{-i\pi}\cos(\sqrt{r}\pi)\big|=2.$
So, $f_{u,u}(\pi)=2$ for all even perfect square $n\geq 4$.
\item Let $u,v$ be vertices of degree $r$ in $X=K_{2,r}$. One checks that $U_X(\frac{\pi}{\sqrt{2r}})_{u,v}=-1$ and $U_{X^c}(\frac{\pi}{\sqrt{2}})_{u,v}=i\sin(\frac{\pi}{\sqrt{2r}})$. Hence, $f_{u,v}\big(\frac{\pi}{\sqrt{2r}}\big)=
\big|i\sin(\frac{\pi}{\sqrt{2r}})+e^{-i\frac{\pi}{\sqrt{2r}}}\big|=\big|\cos(\frac{\pi}{\sqrt{2r}})\big|.$
So, 
$\lim_{r\rightarrow\infty}f_{u,v}(\frac{\pi}{\sqrt{2r}})=1$.
\end{enumerate}

label: thm:projector upper bound
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{thm:projector upper bound}
If $u,v$ are vertices in a graph $X$, then $f_{u,v}(t) \leq 2\sqrt{P_{u,u}}\sqrt{P_{v,v}}.$
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Applying Lemma~\ref{lem: transition_difference} and the triangle inequality, we have
    \[f_{u,v}(t) \leq \sum_{j = 1}^m\left| (\mathbf{u}_j\mathbf{u}_j^\top)_{u,v}\right|+ \sum_{j=1}^m \left|(\mathbf{v}_j\mathbf{v}_j^\top)_{u,v}\right|.\]
    Of course $\left|(\mathbf{u}_j\mathbf{u}_j^\top)_{u,v}\right|=\left| (\mathbf{u}_j^\top\mathbf e_u)(\mathbf{u}_j^\top\mathbf e_v)\right|$, and so the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality yields
    \[f_{u,v}(t)\leq \sqrt{\sum_{j=1}^m(\mathbf{u}_j^\top\mathbf e_u)^2}\sqrt{\sum_{j=1}^m(\mathbf{u}_j^\top\mathbf e_v)^2} + \sqrt{\sum_{j=1}^m(\mathbf{v}_j^\top\mathbf e_u)^2}\sqrt{\sum_{j=1}^m(\mathbf{v}_j^\top\mathbf e_v)^2}.\]
    Since $P_{u,u}=\sum_{j=1}^m(\mathbf{u}_j^\top\mathbf e_u)^2=\sum_{j=1}^m(\mathbf{v}_j^\top\mathbf e_u)^2$, we obtain \(f_{u,v}(t) \leq 2\sqrt{P_{u,u}}\sqrt{P_{v,v}}\) as claimed.
head: environment

title: Remark
body_md: The number of main eigenvalues of a graph is known to be the largest integer $m$ such that the set $\{\mathbf 1, A\mathbf 1,A^2\mathbf 1, \dots, A^{m-1}\mathbf 1\}$ is linearly independent \cite[Proposition 2.2]{rowlinson2007maineigenvaluesurvery}. Hence, Theorem~\ref{thm:projector upper bound} can be applied to any graph $X$ without knowing the spectral decomposition of $A(X)$ or $A(X^c)$.
head: environment

label: prop:2mainevec
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{prop:2mainevec}
Let $X$ be a connected graph. Then $A(X)$ has exactly two linearly independent main eigenvectors if and only if $A(X)$ has exactly two main eigenvalues that are both simple. In this case, one of the main eigenvectors is a Perron eigenvector.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md: Let $\mathbf u$ and $\mathbf v$ be the two linearly independent main eigenvectors of $A(X)$. Since a Perron eigenvector has all positive entries, it follows that it is a main eigenvector, and hence it must be one of $\mathbf u$ or $\mathbf v$. Suppose $\mathbf u$ is a Perron eigenvector and $\mathbf v$ is a main eigenvector for some eigenvalue $\lambda$. If $\lambda$ has multiplicity at least two, then Proposition~\ref{prop:maineigsp} and the fact that the eigenvectors of a symmetric matrix corresponding to distinct eigenvalues are orthogonal imply that there are at least three linearly independent main eigenvectors, a contradiction. Thus, $\lambda$ is a simple eigenvalue of $A(X)$. The converse is immediate.
head: environment

label: thm:nonreguv
title: Theorem
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Recall that the image of $P$ has basis $\{\mathbf 1,A\mathbf 1\}$. The set $\left\{\frac{\mathbf 1}{\sqrt{n}},\frac{A\mathbf 1 - d_{avg}\mathbf 1}{\sqrt{\sum_{w\in V(X)}(d_w-d_{avg})^2}}\right\}$ is an orthonormalization of $\{\mathbf 1,A\mathbf 1\}$, which we use to compute $P$. We find that
    \[P_{u,u} = \frac{1}{n} + \frac{(d_u-d_{avg})^2}{\sum_{w\in V(X)}(d_w-d_{avg})^2}.\]
The claim then follows from this fact and Theorem~\ref{thm:projector upper bound}.
head: environment

title: Remark
body_md: In Theorem~\ref{thm:nonreguv}, if $u,v$ both have average degree, then the upper bound for $f_{u,v}(t)$ coincides with that in Theorem~\ref{thm:regupperbound}. However, if at least one of $u,v$ has degree not equal to the average degree, then Theorem~\ref{thm:nonreguv} yields a larger upper bound for $f_{u,v}(t)$ than that in Theorem~\ref{thm:regupperbound}.
head: environment

label: cor:twomain bidegree bound
title: Corollary
body_md:
\label{cor:twomain bidegree bound}
    Let $X$ be a $n_1+n_2$ vertex graph with exactly two linearly independent main eigenvectors, $n_1$ vertices of degree $k$, and $n_2$ vertices of degree $\ell$. Then 
    \[f_{u,v}(t) \leq \begin{cases}
        2/n_1, &d_u=d_v=k\\
        2/n_2, &d_u=d_v=\ell\\
        2/\sqrt{n_1n_2}&d_u\neq d_v.\\
    \end{cases}\]
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md: Note that $d_{avg} = \frac{n_1k + n_2\ell}{n_1+n_2}$. If $d_u=k$, then $(d_u-d_{avg})^2 = \frac{n_2^2(k-\ell)^2}{(n_1+n_2)^2}$. If $d_u=\ell$, then $(d_u-d_{avg})^2 = \frac{n_1^2(k-\ell)^2}{(n_1+n_2)^2}$. Observe that $\sum_{w\in V(X)}(d_w-d_{avg})^2 = \frac{n_1n_2(k-\ell)^2}{(n_1+n_2)}$. The expression $1+\frac{n(d_u-d_{avg})^2}{\sum_{w\in V(X)}(d_w-d_{avg})^2}$ then simplifies to $1+\frac{n_2}{n_1}$ if $d_u=k$, and $1+\frac{n_1}{n_2}$ if $d_u=\ell$. The claim follows from this and Theorem~\ref{thm:nonreguv}.
head: environment

label: ex:projectorboundonjoin
title: Example
body_md:
\label{ex:projectorboundonjoin}
Let $X,Y$ be $k,\ell$-regular graphs on $n_1,n_2$ vertices, respectively. If $k+n_2=\ell+n_1$, then $X\lor Y$ is regular and $f_{u,v}(t)\leq \frac{2}{n_1+n_2}$ by Theorem~\ref{thm:regupperbound}. If $k+n_2\neq \ell+n_1$, then $X\lor Y$ is irregular with all vertices having degree $k+n_2$ or $\ell+n_1$, and $A(X\lor Y)$ has exactly two linearly independent main eigenvectors. Thus,  Corollary $\ref{cor:twomain bidegree bound}$ grants us bounds for $f_{u,v}(t)$. When $u,v$ both belong to $X$ or to $Y$, Corollary~\ref{cor:joinfuvupperbound} and Corollary~\ref{cor:twomain bidegree bound} yield the same upper bound. When $u\in V(X)$ and $v\in V(Y)$, $U_{(X\lor Y)^c}(t)_{u,v}  = 0$, so $f_{u,v}(t) = \big|U_{X\lor Y}(t)_{u,v}\big|$. By Theorem~\ref{thm:peakstjoin1}, $f_{u,v}(t) \leq 2/\sqrt{(k-\ell)^2+4n_1n_2}$. In this case Corollary~\ref{cor:twomain bidegree bound} yields the larger upper bound $f_{u,v}(t)\leq 2/\sqrt{n_1n_2}$.

title: Proposition
body_md: If $u\neq v$, then $\displaystyle\inf_{t>0}\rho_{u,v}(t)=0$. Moreover, if $u$ is not sedentary in $X$, then $\displaystyle\inf_{t>0}\rho_{u,u}(t)=0$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Since each vertex is almost periodic in $X$, $\sup_{t>0}\lvert U_X(t)_{u,u}\rvert=1$. So, by the unitarity of $U_X(t)$, $\inf_{t>0}\lvert U_X(t)_{u,v}\rvert=0$ if $u\neq v$.
If  $u$ is not sedentary in $X$, then $\inf_{t>0}\lvert U_X(t)_{u,u}\rvert=0$. Combining these observations with the fact that for all $u,v\in V(X)$, $\rho_{u,v}(t)\leq U_X(t)_{u,v}$ for all $t$ yields the above result.
head: environment

label: prop:NG
title: Proposition
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md: Note that (\ref{eq:peakst1}) follows from (\ref{eq:bounding}). If $X$ is coconnected, then  $B(X)_{u,v},B(X^c)_{u,v}>0$ by Proposition~\ref{prop:B+}. Combining this with (\ref{eq:peakst1}) yields the first two statements in 1. The last two statements follow from the fact that $\sup_{t>0}\sigma_{u,v}(t)=2$ (resp., $\sup_{t>0}\rho_{u,v}(t)=1$ ) if and only if $\lim_{m\rightarrow\infty}|U_X(\tau_m)_{u,v}|=\lim_{m\rightarrow\infty}|U_{X^c}(\tau_m)_{u,v}|=1$ for some $\{\tau_m\}$. Next, combining (\ref{eq:peakst1}) and Proposition~\ref{prop:boundmat} gives us 2. Finally, the assumption in 2 implies that $B(X^c)_{u,v}=0$. So, combining this with (\ref{eq:peakst1}) and Lemma~\ref{lem:joinbound} yields 3.

label: ex:K2r
title: Example
body_md:
\label{ex:K2r}
Let $r=2s^2$ and $u,v$ be vertices of degree $r$ in $X=K_{2,r}$. Then $B(X)_{u,v}=B(X^c)_{u,v}=1$, $U_X(t)_{u,v}=\frac{-1+\cos(2st)}{2}$ and $U_{X^c}(t)_{u,v}=i\sin(t)$. So, $|U_X(t)_{u,v}|=\sin^2(st)$ and $|U_{X^c}(t)_{u,v}|=|\sin t|$ are periodic functions in $t$ with periods $\frac{\pi}{s}$ and $\pi$, respectively. If $s$ is odd, then $|U_X(\frac{\pi}{2})_{u,v}|=|U_{X^c}(\frac{\pi}{2})_{u,v}|=1$, and so $\sigma_{u,v}(\frac{\pi}{2})=2$ and $\rho_{u,v}(\frac{\pi}{2})=1$. If $s$ is even, then for any odd integer $q$, $|U_{X^c}(\frac{q\pi}{2})_{u,v}|=1$ and $|U_X(\frac{q\pi}{2})_{u,v}|=0$, while $|U_{X^c}(\frac{q\pi}{2s})_{u,v}|<1=|U_X(\frac{q\pi}{2s})_{u,v}|$. These calculations imply that $|U_X(t)_{u,v}|$ and $|U_{X^c}(t)_{u,v}|$ do not simultaneously attain 1, and so by Proposition~\ref{prop:NG}, the inequalities in (\ref{eq:peakst1}) are strict. Since the sum and product of $|U_X(t)_{u,v}|$ and $|U_{X^c}(t)_{u,v}|$ are periodic continuous functions, $\sigma_{u,v}(t)$ and $\rho_{u,v}(t)$ both attain their maximum, which are less than 2 and 1, respectively. For instance, if $s=2$, then $\max_{t>0}\sigma_{u,v}(t)\approx 1.736<2$ and $\max_{t>0}\rho_{u,v}(t)\approx 0.7436<1$.

label: cor:pgstsup
title: Corollary
body_md:
\label{cor:pgstsup}
If $X$ and $X^c$ both admit PST between the same pair of vertices $u$ and $v$ at times $\tau$ and $\tau'$ such that $\{1,\frac{\tau'}{\tau}\}$ is a linearly independent set over $\mathbb{Q}$, then $\sup_{t>0}\sigma_{u,v}(t)=2$ and $\sup_{t>0}\rho_{u,v}(t)=1$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md: Taking $Y=X^c$ and $(x,y)=(u,v)$ in Theorem~\ref{thm:pgstpal}, we get $\lim_{r\rightarrow\infty}|U_Y(m_r\tau)_{u,v}|=1$ for some sequence $\{m_r\}$ of odd integers. Since $|U_X(m_r\tau)_{u,v}|=1$, the result follows.

label: ex:p3
title: Example
body_md:
\label{ex:p3}
Let $M=A$, and $X=P_3$ with degree one vertices $u$ and $v$. Then $X$ and $X^c$ admit PST between $u$ and $v$ at times $\tau=\frac{\pi}{\sqrt{2}}$ and $\tau'=\frac{\pi}{2}$, respectively. Since $\{1,\frac{\tau'}{\tau}\}$ is a linearly independent set over $\mathbb{Q}$, Corollary~\ref{cor:pgstsup} yields $\sup_{t>0}\sigma_{u,v}(t)=2$ and $\sup_{t>0}\rho_{u,v}(t)=1$.

label: prop:sigma
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{prop:sigma}
Suppose that vertex $u$ is periodic in $X$ and $X^c$ at the same time. If $|U_X(t)_{u,u}|$ and $|U_{X^c}(t)_{u,u}|$ have no common zeros, then there exists $c>0$ such that $\sigma_{u,u}(t)\geq c$ for all $t\in\mathbb{R}$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md: Note that $\sigma_{u,u}(\tau)=0$ if and only if $|U_X(\tau)_{u,u}|=|U_{X^c}(\tau)_{u,u}|=0$. Thus, if $|U_X(t)_{u,u}|$ and $|U_{X^c}(t)_{u,u}|$ have no common zeros, then $\sigma_{u,u}(\tau)>0$ for all $t$. However, since $|U_X(\tau)_{u,u}|$ and $|U_{X^c}(\tau)_{u,u}|$ are both periodic functions with the same period, it follows that $\sigma_{u,u}(\tau)$ is also periodic. Since $\sigma_{u,u}(\tau)$ is continuous, these observations imply that $\sigma_{u,u}(\tau)$ attains a minimum value $c>0$.
head: environment

title: Example
body_md:
For $M=A$, let $r=2s^2$ where $s$ is even, and let $u,v$ be the vertices of degree $r$ in $X=K_{2,r}$, as in Example~\ref{ex:K2r}. One checks that $|U_X(t)_{u,u}|=\frac{1}{2}(1+\cos(2st))$ and $|U_{X^c}(t)_{u,u}|=|\cos(t)|$, which are periodic functions in $t$. Since the set of zeros of $|U_X(t)_{u,u}|$ and $|U_{X^c}(t)_{u,u}|$ are $\{\frac{p\pi}{2s}:p\ \text{is odd}\}$ and $\{\frac{q\pi}{2}:q\ \text{is odd}\}$, respectively. Since $s$ is even, $|U_X(t)_{u,u}|$ and $|U_{X^c}(t)_{u,u}|$ have no common zeros, and so by Proposition~\ref{prop:sigma}, we have $\sigma_{u,u}(t)>\beta$ for some $\beta>0$. 
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              
For instance, if $s=2$, then $\min_{t>0}\sigma_{u,u} (t)\approx 0.672$.

label: rembsgsedentary
title: Remark
body_md:
\label{rembsgsedentary}
	The complement of an $(\alpha,\beta)$-bidegreed split graph $X$ is an $(m+n-1-\beta,m+n-1-\alpha)$-bidegreed split graph whose adjacency matrix is $A(X^c)=\begin{bmatrix}
	O & \mathbf{1}_m\mathbf{1}_n^\top-B \\ \mathbf{1}_n\mathbf{1}_m^\top-B^\top & \mathbf{J}_n-I_n
	\end{bmatrix}$. Theorem~\ref{thmspecdecombsg} can then be used to find its spectral decomposition. Moreover, since $BB^\top$ is $\beta k$-stochastic, we can deduce the eigenvalues of  $(\mathbf{1}_m\mathbf{1}_n^\top-B)(\mathbf{1}_m\mathbf{1}_n^\top-B)^\top$ from that of $BB^\top$. Observe that $E_{\beta k}=\frac{1}{m}\mathbf{J}_m$ and a simple calculation yields $(\mathbf{1}_m\mathbf{1}_n^\top-B)(\mathbf{1}_m\mathbf{1}_n^\top-B)^\top
	=n\mathbf{1}_m\mathbf{1}_m^\top-\mathbf{1}_m\mathbf{1}_n^\top B^\top -B\mathbf{1}_n\mathbf{1}_m^\top +BB^\top
	=(n-2k)\mathbf{J}_m+BB^\top.$
	If $BB^\top$ is irreducible, then  ${\mathrm{spec}}((n-2k)\mathbf{J}_m+BB^\top)=\{m(n-2k)+\beta k\}\cup{\mathrm{spec}}(BB^\top)\backslash\{\beta k\}$. Otherwise, ${\mathrm{spec}}((n-2k)\mathbf{J}_m+BB^\top)=\{m(n-2k)+\beta k\}\cup{\mathrm{spec}}(BB^\top)$.
	Thus $\mathrm{nspec}((\mathbf{1}_m\mathbf{1}_n^\top-B)(\mathbf{1}_m\mathbf{1}_n^\top-B)^\top)=\mathrm{nspec}(BB^\top)$. Similarly, $\mathrm{nspec}((\mathbf{1}_m\mathbf{1}_n^\top-B)^\top(\mathbf{1}_m\mathbf{1}_n^\top-B))=\mathrm{nspec}(B^\top B).$

body_md: The graph $X$ with adjacency matrix $\begin{bmatrix} \mathbf{J}_m-I_m & B_D\\ B_D^\top & O\end{bmatrix}$ where $B_D$ is the incidence matrix of a $(v=m,b=n,r,k=\beta,\lambda)$-design $D$, is a bidegreed split graph with $\gamma=\frac{(m-\beta)(\alpha-m+1)}{m-1}$ By Theorem~\ref{thmbsgsedentary}, vertices in $C$ (resp. $S$) are sedentary in $X$ and $X^c$ if $m>\sqrt{1+4\gamma}+1$ (resp. $n>\sqrt{1+4\gamma}+1$).

label: corbsgsedentary
title: Corollary
body_md:
\label{corbsgsedentary}
	Let ${X}$ be a bidegreed split graph such that $BB^\top$ (resp. $B^\top B$) is reducible into $k$ subblocks and each irreducible subblock $P_i$ of size $n_i$ satisfies $\mathrm{nspec}(P_i)=\{\gamma_i\}$. Then the vertices in the clique $C$ (resp. $S$) corresponding to the subblock $P_i$ are sedentary in ${X}$ and in ${X}^c$ whenever $n_i>\sqrt{1+\gamma_i}+1$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md: We extend the technique used in the proof of Theorem~\ref{thmbsgsedentary}. We have the following key observations: (i) each irreducible subblock $P_i$ of $BB^\top$ is $\beta k$-stochastic, (ii) $\mathrm{nspec}(BB^\top)=\{\beta k\}\cup\left(\bigcup_i \mathrm{nspec}{(P_i)}\right)$, and (iii) if $\mathbf{x}_i$ is a non-main eigenvector of $P_i$ corresponding to $\gamma_i$, then $\mathbf{x}=[\mathbf{0}^\top\cdots\ \mathbf{0}^\top\mathbf{x}_i^\top\ \mathbf{0}^\top\cdots\mathbf{0}^\top]^\top$, partitioned conformally with the subblocks of $BB^\top$, is a non-main eigenvector for $BB^\top$ corresponding to $\gamma_i$. Now, the sum $\sum_{\mathbf{x}}\mathbf{x}\mathbf{x}^\top$ gives us a block diagonal matrix with all zero blocks except at the $i$th diagonal block which is $I_{n_i}-\frac{1}{n_i}\mathbf{J}_{n_i}$ where $n_i$ is the size of the subblock $P_i$. Via the same argument as in the proof of Theorem~\ref{thmbsgsedentary}, we get $\frac{\lambda^2}{\lambda^2+\gamma_i}\sum_{\mathbf{x}}\mathbf{x}\mathbf{x}^\top=(\frac{1}{2}+\frac{1}{2\sqrt{1+4\gamma_i}})(I_{n_i}-\frac{1}{n_i}\mathbf{J}_{n_i})$ so the diagonal entries corresponding to the vertices in $C$ and the subblock $P_i$ in $E_{\lambda,\gamma_i}$ have value $(\frac{1}{2}+\frac{1}{2\sqrt{1+4\gamma_i}})(1-\frac{1}{n_i})>\frac{1}{2}$ when $n_i>\sqrt{1+4\gamma_i}+1$. The result using $B^\top B$ follows similarly.

title: Example
body_md: Let $X$ be the bidegreed split graph where $B=(\mathbf{J}_{n_1}-I_{n_1})\oplus(\mathbf{J}_{n_1}-I_{n_1})$. We have $BB^\top=B^\top B=((n_1-2)\mathbf{J_{n_1}}+I_{n_1})\oplus((n_1-2)\mathbf{J_{n_1}}+I_{n_1})$ which is reducible. Note that $\mathrm{nspec}(BB^\top)=\{n_1(n_1-2)+1,1\}$ so Theorem~\ref{thmbsgsedentary} does not directly apply. However as $\mathrm{nspec}(((n_1-2)\mathbf{J_{n_1}}+I_{n_1}))=\{1\}$ by Corollary~\ref{corbsgsedentary}, the vertices in $C$ and $S$ corresponding to the block $((n_1-2)\mathbf{J_{n_1}}+I_{n_1})$ are sedentary in $X$ and $X^c$ when $n_i\geq 4>\sqrt{5}+1$. The bidegreed split graph $X$ when $n_1=4$ is illustrated in Fig.~\ref{fig2}.
